text: These risks include, but are not limited to, the inability to identify and acquire suitable sites at advantageous prices; competition in targeted market areas; difficulties in obtaining favorable financing for larger acquisitions or construction projects; difficulties during the acquisition process in discovering some of the liabilities of the businesses that we acquire; difficulties associated with our existing financial controls, information systems, management resources and human resources needed to support our future growth; difficulties with hiring, training and retaining skilled personnel; difficulties in adapting distribution and other operational and management systems to an expanded network of stores; difficulties in adopting, adapting to or changing the business practices, models or processes of stores or chains we acquire; difficulties in obtaining governmental and other third-party consents, permits and licenses needed to operate additional stores; difficulties in obtaining the cost savings and financial improvements we anticipate from future acquired stores; the potential diversion of our management’s attention from focusing on our core business due to an increased focus on acquisitions; and, challenges associated with the consummation and integration of any future acquisition.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Overview
text: Overview

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Overview
text: As of April 30, 2026, Casey’s General Stores, Inc. and its direct and indirect wholly-owned subsidiaries operate convenience stores primarily under the names "Casey's" and "Casey’s General Store" throughout 19 states, approximately half of which are located in Iowa, Missouri and Illinois.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Overview
text: During the third quarter of the prior fiscal year, the Company closed on the acquisition of Fikes Wholesale and Group Petroleum Services (collectively "Fikes"), owner of CEFCO Convenience Stores, which added 198 total stores (the "Fikes acquisition") and a wholesale fuel network.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Overview
text: As of April 30, 2026, there were 2,944 stores in operation.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Overview
text: Approximately 71% of all stores were opened in areas with populations of fewer than 20,000 persons.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Overview
text: The Company competes on the basis of traditional features of convenience store operations such as location, extended hours, product offerings, price and quality of service.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Overview
text: All stores carry a broad selection of food items (which at most stores includes, but is not limited to, prepared foods such as regular and breakfast pizza, donuts, hot breakfast items, and hot and cold sandwiches), beverages, tobacco and nicotine products, groceries, health and beauty aids, automotive products, and other non-food items.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Overview
text: As of April 30, 2026, 241 store locations offered car washes.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Overview
text: In addition, all but six store locations offer fuel.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Overview
text: The Company operates a wholesale network where Casey’s manages wholesale fuel supply agreements to certain dealer sites and other wholesale locations.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Overview
text: The dealer and wholesale locations are not operated by Casey's and are not included in our overall store count.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Overview
text: Approximately 3% of total revenue for the year-ended April 30, 2026 relates to the wholesale fuel network.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Overview
text: The Company’s business is seasonal, and generally experiences higher sales and profitability during the first and second fiscal quarters (May-October), when the weather is warmer across our footprint and guests tend to purchase greater quantities of fuel and certain convenience items such as beer, sports drinks, water, soft drinks and ice.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Long-Term Strategic Plan
text: Long-Term Strategic Plan

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Long-Term Strategic Plan
text: The end of this fiscal year marks the end of the three-year strategic plan originally announced in June 2023.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Long-Term Strategic Plan
text: The plan focused on three enterprise objectives: grow store count, accelerate the food business, and enhance operational efficiency, which are enabled by a strong foundation and Team Member experience.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Long-Term Strategic Plan
text: The Company's plan was based on building on our proud heritage and distinct advantages, to become more contemporary through new capabilities, technology, data, and processes.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Long-Term Strategic Plan
text: The Company performed strongly over the three-year period, compared to the original goals in our plan.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Long-Term Strategic Plan
text: Some of the key highlights include: •Built or acquired 504 additional stores over the three-year period, well above the original goal of 350 stores, •Diluted earnings per share for the year was $19.16, representing an increase of 30.9% from the prior year, and annualized growth of 17.2% over the three-year period, •Casey's Rewards members grew to over 10 million at year-end, and •Continued growth of the prepared food program with the expansion of our bone-in and boneless chicken wings, in a variety of flavors, which were available in approximately 850 stores as of the end of the year.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Long-Term Strategic Plan
text: The Company will introduce a new a three-year strategic plan in June 2026.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Electric Vehicles
text: Electric Vehicles

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Electric Vehicles
text: Casey's continues to implement our electric vehicle ("EV") strategy and our management team remains committed to understanding how the increased demand for, and usage of, EVs impacts consumer behavior across our store footprint and beyond.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Electric Vehicles
text: As consumer demand for alternative fuel options continues to grow, albeit slowly, Casey’s has continued to add EV charging stations across our 19-state footprint.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Electric Vehicles
text: As of April 30, 2026, the Company has 282 charging stations at 64 stores, across 14 states.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Electric Vehicles
text: Our EV growth strategy is currently designed to selectively increase our charging stations at locations within our region where we see higher levels of consumer EV buying trends and demand for EV charging.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Electric Vehicles
text: To date, consumer EV demand within our Midwest footprint has been comparatively lower than the levels along the coasts.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Electric Vehicles
text: As EV demand from our guests increases, we are prepared to strategically integrate charging station options at select stores.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Fiscal 2026 Compared with Fiscal 2025

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Fiscal 2026 Compared with Fiscal 2025
text: Total revenue for fiscal 2026 increased by $1,620,202 (10.2%) compared to the prior fiscal year, primarily driven by $1,034,139 of additional revenue from the Fikes acquisition, during the first six months of fiscal 2026.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Fiscal 2026 Compared with Fiscal 2025
text: Prepared food and dispensed beverage revenue increased by $165,066 (10.2%), due to an increase in same-store sales of 5.2% driven by improved sales of hot sandwiches, bakery, and whole pizzas, as well as an increase of approximately 5.0% due to store growth.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Fiscal 2026 Compared with Fiscal 2025

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Use of Non-GAAP Measures
text: Use of Non-GAAP Measures

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Use of Non-GAAP Measures
text: We define EBITDA as net income before net interest expense, income taxes, and depreciation and amortization.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Use of Non-GAAP Measures
text: EBITDA is not considered to be a GAAP measure and should not be considered as a substitute for net income, cash flows from operating activities or other income or cash flow statement data.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Use of Non-GAAP Measures
text: This measure has limitations as an analytical tool, and should not be considered in isolation or as a substitute for analysis of our results as reported under GAAP.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Use of Non-GAAP Measures
text: We strongly encourage investors to review our financial statements and publicly filed reports in their entirety and not to rely on any single financial measure.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Use of Non-GAAP Measures
text: We believe EBITDA is useful to investors in evaluating our operating performance because securities analysts and other interested parties use this calculation as a measure of financial performance and debt service capabilities, and it is regularly used by management for internal purposes including our capital budgeting process, evaluating acquisition targets, assessing store performance, and awarding incentive compensation.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Use of Non-GAAP Measures
text: Because non-GAAP financial measures are not standardized, EBITDA, as defined by us, may not be comparable to similarly titled measures reported by other companies.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Use of Non-GAAP Measures
text: It therefore may not be possible to compare our use of this non-GAAP financial measure with those used by other companies.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Critical Accounting Policies and Estimates
text: Critical Accounting Policies and Estimates

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Critical Accounting Policies and Estimates
text: Critical accounting policies are those accounting policies that management believes are important to the portrayal of our financial condition and results of operations and require management’s most difficult, subjective judgments, often because of the need to estimate the effects of inherently uncertain factors.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Business Combinations
text: Business Combinations

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Business Combinations
text: The Company uses the acquisition method of accounting for transactions meeting the definition of a business combination.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Business Combinations
text: The acquisitions are recorded in the financial statements by allocating the purchase price to the assets acquired, including intangible assets, and liabilities assumed, based on their estimated fair values at the acquisition date as determined by third party appraisals or internal estimates.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Business Combinations
text: The significant assets acquired include buildings, equipment, land, and right-of-use lease assets.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Business Combinations
text: The Company primarily values buildings and equipment using the cost method and land using comparable land sales.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Business Combinations
text: The purchase price is determined based upon the fair value of consideration transferred to the seller.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Business Combinations
text: Fair values are typically determined using Level 3 inputs (see Note 3 to the consolidated financial statements).

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Business Combinations
text: Given these estimates often are based upon unobservable inputs, the estimates require significant judgment when determining the overall value and actual results could differ from the estimates originally established.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Business Combinations
text: When acquiring leases in a business combination, we retain the lease classification utilized by the seller if it was determined using acceptable methods under ASC 842.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Business Combinations
text: As part of the allocation of the purchase price in a business combination, lease terms are compared to market terms utilizing an income approach to determine if leases are favorable or unfavorable.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Business Combinations
text: Any favorable or unfavorable leasehold interests identified increase (favorable) or reduce (unfavorable) the right-of-use lease asset and are recognized over the life of the related right-of-use asset.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Business Combinations
text: The excess of the cost of the acquisition over the net amounts assigned to the fair value of the assets acquired and the liabilities assumed is recorded as goodwill, if the acquisition is considered to be a business combination.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Business Combinations
text: During a one-year period from the acquisition date, amounts are allowed to be provisional for areas that are expected to be adjusted to their final amounts during the measurement period.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Business Combinations
text: These provisional adjustments are for when the buyer obtains additional information about the facts and circumstances that existed as of the acquisition date.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Business Combinations
text: Subsequent adjustments recorded to provisional balances within the measurement period are recorded in the period in which the adjustment is identified.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Business Combinations
text: Acquisition-related transaction costs are recognized in operating expenses as incurred.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Inventory
text: Inventory

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Inventory
text: Inventories, which consist of merchandise and fuel, are stated at the lower of cost or market.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Inventory
text: For fuel inventories, cost is determined through the use of the first-in, first-out (FIFO) method.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Inventory
text: For merchandise inventories, cost is determined through the use of the last-in, first-out (LIFO) method.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Inventory
text: Inventory valued using the LIFO method of inventory requires judgement when making the determination of appropriate indices to be used for determining price level changes.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Long-lived Assets
text: Long-lived Assets

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Long-lived Assets
text: The Company monitors closed and underperforming stores for an indication that the carrying amount of assets may not be recoverable.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Long-lived Assets
text: If the sum of the expected future undiscounted cash flows is less than the carrying amount of the assets, an impairment loss is recognized to the extent carrying value of the assets exceeds their estimated fair value.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Long-lived Assets
text: Fair value is based on management’s estimate of the price that would be received to sell an asset in an orderly transaction between market participants.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Long-lived Assets
text: The estimate is derived from offers, actual sale or disposition of assets subsequent to year-end, and other indications of fair value, which are considered Level 3 inputs (see Note 3 to the consolidated financial statements).

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Long-lived Assets
text: In determining whether an asset is impaired, assets are grouped at the lowest level for which there are identifiable cash flows that are largely independent of the cash flows of other groups of assets, which for the Company is generally on a store-by-store basis.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Long-lived Assets
text: The Company incurred impairment charges of $9,818 in fiscal 2026, $4,080 in fiscal 2025, and $4,057 in fiscal 2024.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Long-lived Assets
text: Impairment charges are a component of operating expenses.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Self-insurance
text: Self-insurance

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Self-insurance
text: The Company is primarily self-insured for Team Member healthcare, workers’ compensation, general liability, and automobile claims.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Self-insurance
text: The self-insurance claim liability for workers’ compensation, general liability, and automobile claims is determined actuarially at each year-end based on claims filed and an estimate of claims incurred but not yet reported.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Self-insurance
text: Actuarial projections of the losses are employed due to the potential of variability in the liability estimates.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Self-insurance
text: Some factors affecting the uncertainty of claims include the development time frame, settlement patterns, litigation and adjudication direction, and medical treatment and cost trends.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Self-insurance
text: The liability is not discounted.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Self-insurance
text: The self-insurance reserves were $67,240 and $74,471 as of April 30, 2026 and 2025, respectively.

text: Due to the nature of our business, cash provided by operations is our primary source of liquidity.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: The Company finances our inventory purchases primarily from normal trade credit aided by relatively rapid inventory turnover.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: This turnover allows us to conduct operations without large amounts of cash and working capital.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: On October 30, 2024, the Company entered into an amendment to the credit agreement (the “Amendment” and, together with the original credit agreement, the “Credit Agreement”), pursuant to which the Company incurred an incremental term loan in an aggregate principal amount of $850,000 (the “Incremental Term Loan”).

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: Amounts borrowed under the Credit Agreement bear interest at variable rates based upon, at the Company’s option, either: (a) either Term SOFR or Daily Simple SOFR, in each case plus 0.10% (with a floor of 0.00%) for the interest period in effect, plus an applicable margin ranging from 1.10% to 1.70% or (b) an alternate base rate, which generally equals the highest of (i) the prime commercial lending rate announced by the Administrative Agent as its “prime rate”, (ii) the federal funds rate plus 1/2 of 1.00%, and (iii) Adjusted Daily Simple SOFR plus 1.00%, each plus an applicable margin ranging from 0.10% to 0.70% and each with a floor of 1.00%.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: The applicable margins and facility fee, in each case, are dependent upon the Company’s quarterly Consolidated Leverage Ratio, as defined in the Credit Agreement.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: We have the right at any time to prepay all or a portion of the outstanding balance without premium or penalty, other than customary “breakage” costs with respect to Term SOFR-based borrowings, with prior notice given.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Overview
text: Overview

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Overview
text: As of July 31, 2026, Casey’s General Stores, Inc. and its direct and indirect wholly-owned subsidiaries operate convenience stores primarily under the names "Casey's" and "Casey’s General Store" (collectively, with the stores below referenced as "GoodStop (by Casey's)" ("GoodStop"), or "CEFCO", referred to as "Casey's" or the "Company") throughout 19 states, approximately half of which are located in Iowa, Missouri and Illinois.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Overview
text: As of July 31, 2026, there were 2,959 stores in operation.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Overview
text: Approximately 71% of all stores were opened in areas with populations of fewer than 20,000 persons.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Overview
text: The Company competes on the basis of traditional features of convenience store operations such as location, extended hours, product offerings, price and quality of service.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Overview
text: All stores carry a broad selection of food items (which at most stores includes, but is not limited to, prepared foods such as regular and breakfast pizza, donuts, hot breakfast items, and hot and cold sandwiches), beverages, tobacco and nicotine products, groceries, health and beauty aids, automotive products, and other non-food items.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Overview
text: As of July 31, 2026, 240 store locations offered car washes.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Overview
text: In addition, all but five store locations offer fuel.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Overview
text: In addition to the "Casey's" and "Casey's General Stores" brands, the Company also operates a limited number of stores under the additional brands of "GoodStop" or "CEFCO".

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Overview
text: These locations offer fuel for sale, and a broad selection of snacks, beverages, tobacco and nicotine products, and other essentials.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Overview
text: However, some of these locations do not have a full-service kitchen and, therefore, have limited prepared food offerings.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Overview
text: When the Company acquires stores, the locations are typically re-branded as "Casey’s" as soon as the store is remodeled to include a full-service kitchen.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Overview
text: If the store’s layout or location does not allow for a full-service kitchen, the store typically will be operated as "GoodStop" or the acquired brand.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Overview
text: The Company operates a wholesale network where Casey’s manages wholesale fuel supply agreements to certain dealer sites and other wholesale locations.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Overview
text: The dealer and wholesale locations are not operated by Casey's and are not included in our overall store count.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Overview
text: For the three-months ended July 31, 2026, approximately 3% of total revenue relates to the wholesale fuel network.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Overview
text: The Company operates three distribution centers, through which certain grocery and general merchandise and prepared food and dispensed beverage items are supplied to most of our stores.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Overview
text: One distribution center is adjacent to our corporate headquarters, which we refer to as the Store Support Center, in Ankeny, Iowa.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Overview
text: The other two distribution centers are located in Terre Haute, Indiana and Joplin, Missouri.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Overview
text: Certain stores outside of our optimal distribution radius, in Florida for example, are supplied by third-party distribution partners.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Overview
text: Additionally, the Company owns and operates a fuel terminal in Waco, Texas.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Overview
text: The Company self-distributes the majority of fuel to our stores.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Overview
text: The Company’s business is seasonal, and generally experiences higher sales and profitability during the first and second fiscal quarters (May-October), when guests tend to purchase greater quantities of fuel and certain convenience items such as beer, sports drinks, water, soft drinks and ice.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Overview

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Electric Vehicles and Renewable Fuels
text: Electric Vehicles and Renewable Fuels

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Electric Vehicles and Renewable Fuels
text: Casey's continues to implement our electric vehicle ("EV") strategy and our management team remains committed to understanding how the increased demand for, and usage of, EVs impacts consumer behavior across our store footprint and beyond.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Electric Vehicles and Renewable Fuels
text: As consumer demand for alternative fuel options continues to grow, albeit slowly, Casey’s has continued to add EV charging stations across our 19-state footprint.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Electric Vehicles and Renewable Fuels
text: As of July 31, 2026, the Company has 294 charging stations at 68 stores, across 14 states.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Electric Vehicles and Renewable Fuels
text: Our EV growth strategy is currently designed to selectively increase our charging stations at locations within our region where we see higher levels of consumer EV buying trends and demand for EV charging.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Electric Vehicles and Renewable Fuels
text: To date, consumer EV demand within our Midwest footprint has been comparatively lower than the levels along the coasts.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Electric Vehicles and Renewable Fuels
text: As EV demand from our guests increases, we are prepared to strategically integrate charging station options at select stores.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Same-Store Sales
text: Same-Store Sales

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Same-Store Sales
text: Same-store sales is a common metric used in the convenience store industry.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Same-Store Sales
text: We define same-store sales as the total sales increase (or decrease) for stores open during the full time of both periods being presented.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Same-Store Sales
text: When comparing data, the store must be open for each entire fiscal period being compared.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Same-Store Sales
text: Remodeled stores that remained open or were closed for just a very brief period of time (i.e., less than a week) during the period being compared remain in the same-store sales comparison.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Same-Store Sales
text: If a store is replaced, either at the same location (i.e., razed and rebuilt) or relocated to a new location, it is removed from the comparison until the new store has been open for each entire period being compared.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Same-Store Sales
text: Newly constructed and acquired stores do not enter the calculation until they are open for each entire period being compared.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Same-Store Sales
text: Same-store sales of prepared food and dispensed beverage increased 4.8% and grocery and general merchandise increased 2.7% during the quarter.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Same-Store Sales
text: The increase in prepared food and dispensed beverage same-store sales was driven primarily by positive traffic, led by whole pizzas.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Same-Store Sales
text: The increase in grocery and general merchandise same-store sales was primarily due to strong sales of non-alcoholic beverages.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Same-Store Sales
text: Additionally, the first quarter results reflected a 0.3% decrease in same-store fuel gallons sold.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Use of Non-GAAP Measures
text: Use of Non-GAAP Measures

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Use of Non-GAAP Measures
text: We define EBITDA as net income before net interest expense, income taxes, and depreciation and amortization.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Use of Non-GAAP Measures
text: EBITDA is not considered to be a GAAP measure, and should not be considered as a substitute for net income, cash flows from operating activities or other income or cash flow statement data.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Use of Non-GAAP Measures
text: This measure has limitations as an analytical tool, and should not be considered in isolation or as a substitute for analysis of our results as reported under GAAP.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Use of Non-GAAP Measures
text: We strongly encourage investors to review our financial statements and publicly filed reports in their entirety and not to rely on any single financial measure.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Use of Non-GAAP Measures

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Business Segments
text: Business Segments

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Business Segments
text: Commencing in the second quarter of fiscal 2026, we implemented a new segment reporting structure which resulted in four reportable segments: North American Pharmaceutical, Oncology & Multispecialty, Prescription Technology Solutions, and Medical-Surgical Solutions.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Business Segments
text: Our former Norwegian operations were included in Other.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Business Segments
text: All prior segment information has been recast to reflect the Company’s new segment structure and current period presentation.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Business Segments
text: Our North American Pharmaceutical segment distributes branded, generic, specialty, biosimilar and over-the-counter (“OTC”) pharmaceutical drugs, and other healthcare-related products to customers in the United States (“U.S.”) and Canada.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Business Segments
text: In addition, the segment sells financial, operational, and clinical solutions to pharmacies (retail, hospital, alternate sites) and provides consulting, outsourcing, technological, and other services.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Business Segments
text: The U.S. distribution operations were previously included in the former U.S. Pharmaceutical reportable segment, and the Canadian operations were previously included in the former International reportable segment.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Business Segments
text: Our Oncology & Multispecialty segment includes provider solutions that encompass specialty drug distribution, group purchasing organizations, infusion services, direct to patient pharmacy capabilities, InspiroGene™ cell and gene therapy services, technology solutions, practice consulting services, and vaccine distribution.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Business Segments
text: In addition, the segment supports the U.S. Oncology Network, one of the largest networks of physician-led, integrated, community-based oncology practices dedicated to advancing high-quality, evidence-based cancer care in the U.S.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Business Segments
text: The segment also includes PRISM Vision Holdings, LLC (“PRISM Vision”); which drives patient outcomes in a retina and ophthalmology setting.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Business Segments
text: Combined with Sarah Cannon Research Institute (“SCRI”) and our technology business, Ontada, this segment provides research, insights, technologies, and services that address and improve cancer and specialty care.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Business Segments
text: This segment was previously reflected in the former U.S. Pharmaceutical reportable segment.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Business Segments
text: Our Prescription Technology Solutions segment helps solve medication access, affordability, and adherence challenges for patients by working across healthcare to connect patients, pharmacies, providers, pharmacy benefit managers, health plans, and biopharma companies.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Business Segments
text: Prescription Technology Solutions serves our biopharma and life sciences partners, delivering innovative solutions that help people get the medicine they need to live healthier lives.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Business Segments
text: Prescription Technology Solutions offers technology services, which includes electronic prior authorization, prescription price transparency, benefit insight, dispensing support services, and patient enrollment, in addition to third-party logistics and wholesale distribution support designed to benefit stakeholders.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Business Segments
text: Our Medical-Surgical Solutions segment is a leading provider of medical-surgical supplies, laboratory equipment, and pharmaceutical distribution, logistics, and other services to non-acute settings in the U.S.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Business Segments
text: These include healthcare providers operating in ambulatory care environments, such as physician offices, surgery centers, and hospital reference labs, as well as extended care settings, including nursing homes, hospice and home health care agencies, government markets, and online marketplaces and retailers.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Business Segments
text: This segment offers more than 270,000 national brand medical-surgical products as well as its own line of more than 4,000 high-quality products through a network of distribution centers in the U.S.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Business Segments
text: During fiscal 2026, we announced our intention to separate this segment into an independent company.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Business Segments
text: As a part of the separation strategy, on April 20, 2026, we announced a definitive agreement under which funds managed by affiliates of Apollo Global Management, Inc. (“Apollo Funds”) will acquire approximately 13% minority ownership interest in our Medical‑Surgical Solutions segment through an investment of approximately $1.25 billion in the segment’s convertible preferred equity.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Business Segments
text: This transaction is subject to regulatory approvals and customary closing conditions.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > North American Pharmaceutical Segment
text: North American Pharmaceutical Segment:

section_path: Part I Item 1 > North American Pharmaceutical Segment
text: Our North American Pharmaceutical segment provides distribution and logistics services for branded, generic, specialty, biosimilar, and OTC pharmaceutical drugs along with other healthcare-related products to customers in the U.S. and Canada.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > North American Pharmaceutical Segment
text: This business provides solutions and services to pharmacies, hospitals, pharmaceutical manufacturers, physicians, payors, and patients.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > North American Pharmaceutical Segment
text: We also source generic pharmaceutical drugs through our ClarusONE Sourcing Services LLP joint venture with Walmart Inc. (“ClarusONE”).

section_path: Part I Item 1 > U.S. Pharmaceutical
text: U.S. Pharmaceutical

section_path: Part I Item 1 > U.S. Pharmaceutical
text: Our U.S. Pharmaceutical business operates and serves customers through a network of 27 distribution centers in the U.S., including two strategic redistribution centers.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > U.S. Pharmaceutical
text: We invest in technology and other systems at all of our distribution centers to enhance safety, reliability, and product availability.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > U.S. Pharmaceutical
text: For example, we offer McKesson ConnectSM, an internet-based ordering system that provides item look-up and real-time inventory availability as well as ordering, purchasing, third-party reconciliation, and account management functionality.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > U.S. Pharmaceutical
text: We make extensive use of technology as an enabler to ensure customers have the right products at the right time in the right place.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > U.S. Pharmaceutical
text: To maximize distribution efficiency and effectiveness, we follow the Six Sigma methodology, which is an analytical approach that emphasizes setting high-quality objectives, collecting data, and analyzing results to a fine degree in order to improve processes, reduce costs, and enhance service accuracy and safety.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > U.S. Pharmaceutical
text: We provide solutions to our customers including supply management technology, world-class marketing programs, managed care, and services to help them meet their business and quality goals.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > U.S. Pharmaceutical
text: We continue to implement information systems to help achieve greater consistency and accuracy both internally and for our customers, as well as make investments to increase capacity and automation.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > U.S. Pharmaceutical
text: Within U.S. Pharmaceutical, we have three primary pharmaceutical distribution customer channels: (i) retail national accounts, which include national and regional retail chains, food and drug combinations, mail order pharmacies, and mass merchandisers, (ii) community pharmacy and health, and (iii) institutional healthcare providers such as hospitals, health systems, integrated delivery networks, and long-term care providers.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > U.S. Pharmaceutical
text: Retail National Accounts: We provide business solutions that help our retail national account customers increase revenues and profitability.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > U.S. Pharmaceutical
text: Solutions include:

section_path: Part I Item 1 > U.S. Pharmaceutical
text: Central FillSM – Prescription refill service that enables pharmacies to more quickly refill prescriptions remotely, more accurately, and at a lower cost, while reducing inventory levels and improving customer service.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > U.S. Pharmaceutical
text: Strategic Redistribution Centers – Two facilities totaling over 740,000 square feet that offer access to inventory for single source warehouse purchasing, including pharmaceuticals and biologics.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > U.S. Pharmaceutical
text: These distribution centers also provide the foundation for a two-tiered distribution network that supports best-in-class direct store delivery.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > U.S. Pharmaceutical
text: McKesson SynerGx® – Generic pharmaceutical purchasing program and inventory management that helps pharmacies maximize their cost savings with a broad selection of generic drugs, competitive pricing, and one-stop shopping.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > U.S. Pharmaceutical
text: Inventory Management – An integrated solution comprised of forecasting software and automated replenishment technologies that reduce inventory-carrying costs.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > U.S. Pharmaceutical
text: ExpressRx Track™ – Pharmacy automation solution featuring state-of-the-art robotics, upgraded imaging, and expanded vial capabilities, and industry-leading speed and accuracy in a small footprint.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > U.S. Pharmaceutical
text: Community Pharmacy and Health: We strengthen the overall health of community pharmacies and elevate the role they play in people’s lives.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > U.S. Pharmaceutical
text: We accomplish this by providing supply chain excellence, pharmacy and patient solutions, as well as supporting independent pharmacies through industry and legislative advocacy.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > U.S. Pharmaceutical
text: Our pharmacy and patient solutions include:

section_path: Part I Item 1 > U.S. Pharmaceutical
text: Health Mart® – A national network of approximately 3,900 independently-owned pharmacies and one of the industry’s most comprehensive pharmacy franchise programs.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > U.S. Pharmaceutical
text: Health Mart provides solutions for franchisees to promote excellence in business operations, team development, patient health, marketing and merchandising, and protects financial health through proactive audit support.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > U.S. Pharmaceutical
text: Health Mart Atlas® and Atlas Specialty – Comprehensive managed care services that connect the continuum of care to help community pharmacies, health systems, and physician practices save time, access competitive reimbursement rates, and improve cash flow.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > U.S. Pharmaceutical
text: McKesson Reimbursement AdvantageSM (“MRA”) – MRA is one of the industry’s most comprehensive reimbursement optimization packages, comprising financial services (automated claim resubmission), analytic services, and customer care.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > U.S. Pharmaceutical
text: McKesson Provider Pay® – An automated reconciliation and payment management solution designed to maximize third-party cash flow and pursue unpaid claims.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > U.S. Pharmaceutical
text: McKesson Amplify – Provides resources for state pharmacy associations in all 50 states, including dedicated support funding, resources, and opportunities to participate in best practice sharing consortia.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > U.S. Pharmaceutical
text: The funding helps to support advocacy initiatives that address the unique challenges faced by independent pharmacies and promote their sustainability and growth.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > U.S. Pharmaceutical
text: McKesson OneStop Generics® – Generic pharmaceutical purchasing program that helps pharmacies maximize their cost savings with a broad selection of generic drugs, competitive pricing, and one-stop shopping.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > U.S. Pharmaceutical
text: Pinpoint Community Solutions – McKesson’s perpetual inventory management system targeted to independent pharmacy owners with five or fewer stores.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > U.S. Pharmaceutical

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Competition

text: We operate in highly competitive markets across North America, and the healthcare industry has experienced significant consolidation in recent years.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: Government Regulation

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: We operate in many highly regulated environments and are subject to oversight by various federal, state, and local governmental entities in the U.S. and elsewhere.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: We incur significant expense and make large capital expenditures and investments to enable us to comply with laws and guidance promulgated by governmental entities.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: The regulatory framework affecting our business and industry is continually evolving and influenced by conditions such as public policy developments; shifts in governmental priorities, initiatives, and focus areas, including due to changes in federal, state, and local representation; and varied interpretations of laws and agency rulemaking conventions.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: These conditions create uncertainties for our business, and we are unable to predict the impact of future changes to the regulatory framework, or any prolonged uncertainty, on our operations and compliance costs.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: See “Risk Factors” in Item 1A of Part I below for additional information regarding material risks associated with our compliance with governmental regulations.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: Operational Licenses and Permits; Controlled Substances: We are subject to the operating and security standards of the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (“DEA”), the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (“FDA”), the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (“HHS”), the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (“CMS”), various state boards of pharmacy, state health departments, and comparable agencies in the U.S. and other countries.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: Certain of our businesses may be required to register for permits and/or licenses with governmental agencies, depending upon the type of operations and location of product development, manufacture, distribution, and sale.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: For example, we are required to hold valid DEA and state-level registrations and licenses, meet various security and operating standards, and comply with the Controlled Substances Act and its accompanying regulations governing the sale, marketing, packaging, holding, distribution, and disposal of controlled substances.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: We maintain extensive controlled substance monitoring and reporting programs at considerable expense in order to help us meet those standards.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: Government Contracts: Our contracts with governmental entities typically are subject to procurement laws that include socio-economic, employment practices, environmental protection, recordkeeping and accounting, and other requirements.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: These statutory and regulatory requirements complicate our business and increase our compliance burden.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: We are subject to audits, investigations, and oversight proceedings about our compliance with contractual and legal requirements.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: Healthcare Program Regulation: Federal, state, and local governmental entities in the U.S. and elsewhere continue to strengthen their position on, and scrutiny of, practices that they believe may indicate fraud, waste, and abuse affecting government healthcare programs such as Medicare and Medicaid.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: Our relationships with pharmaceutical and medical-surgical product manufacturers, healthcare providers, and other companies and individuals, as well as our provision of products and services to governmental entities, subject our business to statutes, regulations, and government guidance that are intended to prevent fraud and abuse.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: Among other things, those laws: (1) prohibit persons from soliciting, offering, receiving, or paying any remuneration in order to induce the referral of an individual for, or to induce the ordering or purchasing of, items or services that are in any way paid for by Medicare, Medicaid, or other government healthcare programs; (2) prohibit physicians from referring certain “designated health services” to an entity with which they have a financial relationship, unless an exception applies; (3) prohibit knowingly submitting, or causing to be submitted, a false or fraudulent claim for payment to the government; and (4) require certain entities to report and return an overpayment by Medicare or Medicaid within 60 days of identifying the overpayment.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: Many of these healthcare fraud and abuse laws are vague or indefinite, and are often subject to varied and evolving interpretations by courts, regulators, and enforcing agencies and, as such, may be interpreted or applied by a prosecutorial, regulatory, or judicial authority in a manner that could require us to make changes in our operations at added expense.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: The healthcare industry continues to be impacted by reform efforts aimed at reducing costs and government spending, as well as by challenges to those efforts.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: In the U.S., the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act (“ACA”) significantly expanded health insurance coverage to uninsured Americans and changed the way healthcare is financed by both governmental and private payors.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: The ACA has faced scrutiny since its adoption, and we cannot predict the impact of any initiatives to change or repeal its provisions.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: Further, the ACA’s enhanced premium subsidies expired on December 31, 2025, and remain subject to ongoing Congressional review.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: The nonrenewal of, or any modifications to, these subsidies may reduce the availability of insurance coverage for certain patients and, in turn, impact our customers and our business.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: The Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 (“IRA”) made meaningful changes affecting benefit design and how Medicare pays for drugs, which are all intended to reduce the price of drugs.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: Three central features of the IRA have authorized the government to negotiate drug prices for certain Medicare Part B and Medicare Part D drugs over time, establish an inflation rebate program, and cap patient cost sharing under Medicare Part D. The ongoing implementation of the IRA may significantly affect the pharmaceutical value chain as manufacturers, pharmacy benefit managers, managed care organizations, and other stakeholders adapt their business models.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: Considerable uncertainty remains, including due to any future regulations and guidance.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: The One Big Beautiful Bill (“OBBBA”), enacted in July 2025, includes provisions expected to reduce Medicaid enrollment and federal funding to state Medicaid programs, which may limit coverage or payment for products and services and impact the financial stability of our customers.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: Executive Order 14297, “Delivering Most-Favored-Nation Prescription Drug Pricing to American Patients,” issued in May 2025, seeks to facilitate manufacturers’ sale of certain drugs in the U.S. at no higher than the lowest prices paid in other developed countries.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: It also directs HHS to enable direct-to-consumer purchasing programs for prescription drugs at most-favored-nation prices, which may bypass supply chain intermediaries.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: Separately, CMS adopted a rule, effective January 1, 2026, on bona fide service fees (“BFSFs”) paid by drug manufacturers, including wholesaler distribution fees.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: The rule requires manufacturers to obtain certifications from wholesalers and other fee recipients that the fee recipient does not pass on the fee to a client or customer.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: Manufacturers are required to submit these certifications to CMS as part of their quarterly average sales price reporting.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: This rule creates a risk that certifications, when and if given, could be challenged, and that manufacturers may seek modifications to their service agreements.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: CMS waived the initial Q1 2026 reporting deadline that had been set for April 30, 2026.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: As of the date of this report, the form and scope of the certification requirements remain subject to change.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: CMS may also pursue additional changes to BFSF requirements in future rulemaking cycles that may impact fee recipients, including wholesalers.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: CMS also proposed two rules in December 2025 that, if finalized, would implement mandatory manufacturer rebate models for certain Medicare Part B and Medicare Part D drugs based on international pricing benchmarks.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: These models would be tested in select geographic areas over a multi-year trial period.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: There are ongoing developments with respect to the 340B Drug Pricing Program (the “340B program”) administered by the Health Resources and Services Administration (“HRSA”).

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: The 340B program requires manufacturers to offer discounts on certain drugs purchased by “covered entities” such as safety-net providers, and some of our customers are covered entities or contract pharmacies for covered entities.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: Various manufacturers have unilaterally restricted sales under the 340B program to a limited number of contract pharmacies, and these practices are the subject of ongoing litigation.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: Further, HRSA continues to evaluate the potential implementation of a retrospective rebate model to effectuate 340B pricing in lieu of upfront discounts.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: A coalition of covered entities successfully challenged HRSA’s previously proposed rebate model pilot program, which had been scheduled to take effect on January 1, 2026.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: HRSA announced that pilot program amid separate litigation over its refusal to approve alternative rebate models proposed by manufacturers, and this litigation continues.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: These developments could, for example, limit the availability of 340B pricing or discounts for our customers.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: It is uncertain whether other changes to the 340B program may be effected through legislation, regulation, or judicial decision, or whether manufacturers will reduce their participation in or take other approaches to the 340B program.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: The cumulative impact of the foregoing on our customers and our business is difficult to predict.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: Additionally, some states have enacted or are considering laws imposing caps or limits on the price of certain drugs distributed by wholesalers in those states.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: If upheld or enacted, these laws could encourage similar measures in other jurisdictions and could, directly or indirectly, affect wholesaler distribution economics.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: We continue to monitor these and other state reform initiatives and their potential impact on our business.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: Outside the U.S., provincial governments in Canada that provide partial funding for the purchase of pharmaceuticals and independently regulate the sale and reimbursement of drugs have sought to reduce the costs of publicly funded health programs.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: For example, these governments have taken steps to reduce consumer prices for generic pharmaceuticals and, in some provinces, change professional allowances paid to pharmacists by generic drug manufacturers.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: FDA Regulation and Supply Chain Integrity: In the U.S., the FDA is the principal federal authority that regulates the safety, efficacy, quality, testing, premarket approval, manufacture, labeling, storage, distribution, and post-market surveillance of healthcare products, such as drugs and medical devices, foods, and cosmetics.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: Federal and state laws regulate the pharmaceutical drug supply chain in order to prevent the distribution of counterfeit, stolen, contaminated, or otherwise harmful prescription drugs in interstate commerce.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: At the federal level, the Drug Supply Chain Security Act (“DSCSA”), among other things, requires standardized, unit-level traceability of pharmaceutical products along the entire drug supply chain and requires all trading partners to cooperate in an electronic, interoperable prescription drug traceability system.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: The DSCSA also sets forth national standards for the licensure of wholesale drug distributors and third-party logistic providers and other requirements applicable to these entities and the FDA has issued a proposed rule with respect to these requirements.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: These federal and state regulatory requirements have increased, and may further increase, our compliance burden and distribution costs.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: Additionally, federal and state governments may adopt other laws intended to protect the integrity of the supply chain, and those laws could affect our distribution business.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: For example, the Federal Trade Commission (“FTC”) and HHS issued a request for public comment in 2024 on how the practices of pharmaceutical wholesalers and group purchasing organizations impact generic drug shortages.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: Various industry stakeholders responded to this request, but no further action has been taken by the FTC or HHS.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: Cybersecurity, Data Security, Privacy, and AI: We are subject to many cybersecurity, privacy, and data protection laws that change frequently and have requirements that vary from jurisdiction to jurisdiction.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: Our efforts to comply with these laws complicate our operations and add to our costs.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: We are subject to significant compliance obligations under privacy laws such as the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996, the General Data Protection Regulation in the European Union, the Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act in Canada, and an expanding list of comprehensive state privacy laws in the U.S.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: Some privacy laws may prohibit the transfer of personal information to certain other jurisdictions or otherwise limit our use and disclosure of data.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: Many of these laws also require us to provide access or other data rights (modification, deletion, portability, etc.) to consumers’ and patients’ individual personal data records within specified periods of time.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: Cybersecurity laws such as the federal Cyber Incident Reporting for Critical Infrastructure Act of 2022, proposed changes to the Federal Acquisition Regulation, and SEC reporting requirements may require us to provide notifications of certain cybersecurity incidents within short timeframes.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: Regulations and guidance targeting critical infrastructure entities, including McKesson, continue to be a focus of regulators.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: We are subject to privacy and data protection compliance audits or investigations by various governmental agencies.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: Additionally, AI laws and guidance are rapidly expanding and changing, with potential differences or conflicts across jurisdictions.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: This creates uncertainty and regulatory risk, including for healthcare-related uses of AI.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: If we or our third-party providers are restricted from using AI as a result of any laws, regulatory views, or other measures, it could impact our operations and competitiveness, increase our compliance expense and burden (including related to any documentation, risk management, or transparency measures), and cause us to modify our use, development, or deployment of AI and incur substantial costs.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: We also could be subject to increased litigation and enforcement risks.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: The cumulative impact of these evolving requirements on our business is difficult to predict.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: Environmental Regulation: We are subject to requirements in various jurisdictions concerning the environment, including laws addressing discharges into the air and water, the management and disposal of hazardous substances and wastes, and the remediation of contaminated sites, as well as laws governing the operation of radiation-emitting equipment at the U.S. Oncology Network practices.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: We sold our chemical distribution operations in 1987 and retained responsibility for certain environmental obligations.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: Agreements with the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and certain states have required and may require environmental assessments and remediation at several sites.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: These matters are described further in Financial Note 17, “Commitments and Contingent Liabilities,” to the consolidated financial statements included in this Annual Report.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: Climate Change Regulation: Governments in the U.S. and abroad have adopted or are considering new or expanded policies and laws to address climate change.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: Such policies and laws may necessitate reductions in greenhouse gas (“GHG”) emissions; mandate that companies implement processes and controls to monitor and disclose climate-related matters; and impose additional taxes or offset charges on specified energy sources, among other requirements.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: Compliance with climate-related policies and laws may be further complicated by disparate regulatory approaches in various jurisdictions.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: New or expanded climate-related policies and laws could impose costs on us, including capital expenditures to develop or modify data gathering and reporting systems, third-party attestations, and additional GHG reduction measures.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: Until the timing and extent of climate-related policies and laws are clarified, including due to legal challenges, we cannot predict their potential effect on our capital expenditures, results of operations, or competitive position.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: Competition and Related Laws: Antitrust and competition laws (“competition laws”) in the U.S. and elsewhere prohibit types of conduct, practices, or arrangements deemed to be anti-competitive.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: Enforcement of competition laws in the healthcare industry remains a focus of the FTC and the U.S. Department of Justice.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: Some of our strategic transactions may require review by competition regulators, with potential delays or other unfavorable outcomes.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: Violations of competition laws can result in sanctions and other adverse actions, including criminal and civil penalties.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: Private plaintiffs also may bring civil lawsuits for alleged violations of competition laws, including claims for treble damages.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: Additionally, laws may be proposed to restrict certain healthcare ownership structures or arrangements, such as vertical integration involving physician practice administrative or management services and pharmaceutical distribution services, where traditional antitrust standards might not be implicated.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Government Regulation
text: Competition and related laws contribute to our compliance efforts and expense, and the enforcement, enactment, expansion, or application of any of the foregoing types of laws might materially adversely affect our operations and growth strategy.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Other Information about the Business
text: Customers: During fiscal 2026, sales to our ten largest customers, including group purchasing organizations (“GPOs”) accounted for approximately 73% of our total consolidated revenues.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Other Information about the Business
text: Sales to our largest customer, CVS Health Corporation (“CVS”), accounted for approximately 24% of our total consolidated revenues in fiscal 2026.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Other Information about the Business
text: In fiscal 2023, we extended our pharmaceutical distribution partnership with CVS to June 2027.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Other Information about the Business
text: Sales to our next two largest customers accounted for 11% and 10% of total consolidated revenues in fiscal 2026.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Other Information about the Business
text: Our ten largest customers comprised approximately 43% of total trade accounts receivable at March 31, 2026.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Other Information about the Business
text: CVS was approximately 21% of our total trade accounts receivable at March 31, 2026.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Other Information about the Business
text: We also have agreements with GPOs, each of which functions as a purchasing agent on behalf of member hospitals, pharmacies, and other healthcare providers, as well as with government entities and agencies.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Other Information about the Business
text: The accounts receivable balances are with individual members of the GPOs, and therefore no significant concentration of credit risk exists.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Other Information about the Business
text: Substantially all of these revenues and accounts receivable are included in our North American Pharmaceutical segment.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Other Information about the Business
text: Suppliers: We obtain pharmaceutical and other products from manufacturers and our largest supplier accounted for 11% of our total purchases in fiscal 2026.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Other Information about the Business
text: The loss of a supplier could adversely affect our business if alternate sources of supply are unavailable.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Other Information about the Business
text: We believe that our relationships with our suppliers are generally sound.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Other Information about the Business
text: The ten largest suppliers in fiscal 2026 accounted for approximately 71% of our total purchases.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Other Information about the Business
text: Some of our distribution arrangements with manufacturers provide us consideration based on a percentage of our purchases.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Other Information about the Business
text: In addition, we have certain distribution arrangements with pharmaceutical manufacturers that include an inflation-based consideration component whereby we benefit when the manufacturers increase their prices as we sell our existing inventory at the new higher prices.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Other Information about the Business
text: For these manufacturers, a reduction in the frequency and magnitude of price increases, as well as restrictions in the amount of inventory available to us, could have an adverse impact on our gross profit margin.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Other Information about the Business
text: Research and Development: Research and development expenses were $103 million, $91 million, and $77 million for the years ended March 31, 2026, 2025, and 2024, respectively.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Company and Operational Risks

text: The risk and efficacy of cyberattacks increases from time to time due to a variety of internal and external factors, including, but not limited to, the use by threat actors of sophisticated and rapidly evolving techniques, such as adversarial AI (which makes cyberattacks more likely and may make them more difficult to detect, contain, or mitigate), and the existence of political or military unrest.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Company and Operational Risks

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Company and Operational Risks

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Company and Operational Risks

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Company and Operational Risks

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Company and Operational Risks

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Company and Operational Risks
category: Company and Operational Risks

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Company and Operational Risks

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Company and Operational Risks

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Company and Operational Risks

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Company and Operational Risks

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Company and Operational Risks

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Industry and Economic Risks
category: Industry and Economic Risks
text: We might be adversely impacted by healthcare reform such as changes in pricing and reimbursement models.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Industry and Economic Risks
category: Industry and Economic Risks
text: Many of our products and services are designed to function within the structure of current healthcare financing and reimbursement systems.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Industry and Economic Risks
category: Industry and Economic Risks
text: The healthcare industry and related government programs continue to change.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Industry and Economic Risks
category: Industry and Economic Risks
text: Some of these changes increase our risks and create uncertainties for our business.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Industry and Economic Risks
category: Industry and Economic Risks
text: For example, certain changes in reimbursement methodologies (including government rates) for pharmaceuticals, medical treatments, and related services reduce profit margins for us and our customers and impose new legal requirements on healthcare providers.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Industry and Economic Risks
category: Industry and Economic Risks
text: Those changes have included cuts in Medicare and Medicaid reimbursement levels, changes in the bases for payments, shifts from fee-for-service pricing towards value-based payments and risk-sharing models, and increases in the use of managed care.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Industry and Economic Risks
category: Industry and Economic Risks
text: As described under “Healthcare Program Regulation” in Item 1 of Part I above, our business is subject to a broad range of recent and ongoing reform efforts, and challenges to those efforts, that could affect healthcare program access and spending, pharmaceutical pricing and reimbursement, and distribution economics.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Industry and Economic Risks
category: Industry and Economic Risks
text: These include: the IRA; the OBBBA; Executive Order 14297; CMS rulemaking on BFSFs and proposed rebate models; 340B program litigation and developments; and state drug pricing legislation.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Industry and Economic Risks
category: Industry and Economic Risks
text: Additionally, the pace and volume of healthcare reform initiatives and changes heighten the risks for our business.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Industry and Economic Risks
category: Industry and Economic Risks
text: There is substantial uncertainty about the likelihood, timing, and results of these healthcare reform efforts and challenges, and their implementation or outcome might have a materially adverse impact on our business operations and our financial position or results of operations.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Industry and Economic Risks
category: Industry and Economic Risks
text: We are adversely impacted by competition and industry consolidation.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Industry and Economic Risks
category: Industry and Economic Risks
text: Our businesses face a highly competitive global environment with strong competition from international, national, regional, and local full-line, short-line, and specialty distributors, service merchandisers, self-warehousing chain drug stores, manufacturers engaged in direct distribution, third-party logistics companies, and large payer organizations.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Industry and Economic Risks
category: Industry and Economic Risks
text: In addition, our businesses face competition from various other service providers and from pharmaceutical and other healthcare manufacturers as well as other potential customers, which may from time to time decide to develop, for their own internal needs, supply management capabilities that might otherwise be provided by our businesses.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Industry and Economic Risks
category: Industry and Economic Risks
text: We also may face competition from companies that move faster to adopt emerging technologies.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Industry and Economic Risks
category: Industry and Economic Risks
text: Due to consolidation, a few large suppliers control a significant share of the pharmaceuticals market.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Industry and Economic Risks

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Industry and Economic Risks
category: Industry and Economic Risks

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Industry and Economic Risks

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Industry and Economic Risks

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Industry and Economic Risks

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Industry and Economic Risks

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Industry and Economic Risks

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Industry and Economic Risks
category: Industry and Economic Risks

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Industry and Economic Risks

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Industry and Economic Risks

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Industry and Economic Risks
category: Industry and Economic Risks

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Industry and Economic Risks

text: In particular, the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development’s Pillar Two initiative introduces a 15% global minimum tax applied on a country-by-country basis which many jurisdictions have enacted or committed to enact.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Industry and Economic Risks

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Industry and Economic Risks

section_path: Part I Item 1A > General Risks
category: General Risks
text: From time to time we are adversely affected by conditions and events outside of our control, including: widespread public health issues such as epidemic or pandemic infectious diseases; natural disasters and other catastrophic events such as earthquakes, floods, or severe weather; and geopolitical factors such as terrorism, military conflicts, civil unrest, political circumstances (including changes in international relations), changes or uncertainty in government policies (including with respect to U.S. or international trade), actual or announced tariffs or other trade restrictions, government shutdowns, or changes in laws or their interpretation.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > General Risks
category: General Risks
text: These conditions and events can disrupt operations for us, our suppliers, our vendors, and our customers, as well as impair product manufacturing, supply, and transport availability and cost in unpredictable ways that depend on highly uncertain future developments.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > General Risks
category: General Risks
text: They might affect consumer confidence levels and spending or the availability of certain goods, commodities, raw materials, and other inputs.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > General Risks
category: General Risks

section_path: Part I Item 1A > General Risks
category: General Risks
text: For example, the trade environment remains highly dynamic and uncertain, and trade policies may be interrelated with other government initiatives.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > General Risks

section_path: Part I Item 1A > General Risks
category: General Risks

section_path: Part I Item 1A > General Risks
category: General Risks

section_path: Part I Item 1A > General Risks
category: General Risks

section_path: Part I Item 1A > General Risks
category: General Risks

section_path: Part I Item 1A > General Risks
category: General Risks
text: Our amended and restated bylaws provide that, unless the Corporation consents in writing to the selection of an alternative forum, the sole and exclusive forum for specified legal actions is the Court of Chancery of the State of Delaware or the United States District Court for the District of Delaware if the Court of Chancery does not have or declines to accept jurisdiction (collectively, “Delaware Courts”).

section_path: Part I Item 1A > General Risks
category: General Risks
text: Current and former stockholders are deemed to have consented to the personal jurisdiction of the Delaware Courts in connection with any action to enforce that exclusive forum provision and to service of process in any such action.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > General Risks
category: General Risks
text: These provisions of the bylaws are not a waiver of, and do not relieve anyone of duties to comply with, federal securities laws including those specifying the exclusive jurisdiction of federal courts under the Exchange Act and concurrent jurisdiction of federal and state courts under the Securities Act.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > General Risks
category: General Risks
text: To the extent that these provisions of the bylaws limit a current or former stockholder’s ability to select a judicial forum other than the Delaware Courts, they might discourage the specified legal actions, might cause current or former stockholders to incur additional litigation-related expenses, and might result in outcomes unfavorable to current or former stockholders.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > General Risks
category: General Risks
text: A court might determine that these provisions of the bylaws are inapplicable or unenforceable in any particular action, in which case we may incur additional litigation related expenses in such action, and the action may result in outcomes unfavorable to us, which could have a materially adverse impact on our reputation, our business operations, and our financial position or results of operations.
