section_path: Part I Item 2 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: In addition to the supply capacity we generate through our proprietary product and process technology that increases bit density per wafer, we will need to add new DRAM wafer capacity to support projected memory demand in the second half of the decade and beyond.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: Following the enactment of the CHIPS Act, we announced plans to invest in leading-edge memory manufacturing sites in Idaho and New York, based on CHIPS Act support through grants and investment tax credits.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: As part of this plan, in September 2022, we broke ground on a leading-edge memory manufacturing fab in Boise, Idaho.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: Construction of the fab began in October 2023, with first DRAM wafer output projected in mid-calendar 2027.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: In June 2025, in connection with certain amendments to our CHIPS Act agreements, we announced plans for a second leading-edge memory manufacturing fab in Idaho to serve growing market demand fueled by AI.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: We plan to begin construction of the second Idaho fab in 2026, and expect initial wafer output by late calendar 2028.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: Our investment plan for New York includes construction of a leading-edge DRAM memory manufacturing site, consisting of up to four fabs to be built over the next 20-plus years, in Clay, New York.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: In January 2026, we broke ground on our first New York fab, which will provide supply in 2030 and beyond.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: We expect these new fabs to be key to meeting our requirements for additional wafer capacity, in line with industry demand trends and our objective of maintaining stable bit share.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: On December 9, 2024, we entered into direct funding agreements with the U.S. Department of Commerce for up to $6.1 billion in direct funding pursuant to the CHIPS Act for a planned fab in Boise, Idaho, and two planned fabs in Clay, New York.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: On June 11, 2025, we entered into amendments to the direct funding agreements to add a second planned fab in Boise, Idaho, and allocate certain award funding to the second planned Idaho fab from the $6.1 billion grants previously awarded under the December 2024 direct funding agreements.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: The direct funding for up to $6.1 billion remains unchanged.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: On June 11, 2025, we also entered into a direct funding agreement with the U.S. Department of Commerce for up to $275 million in direct funding to expand and modernize our fab in Manassas, Virginia.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: The grants under the funding agreements represent total CHIPS Act grants of up to $6.4 billion in connection with our U.S. manufacturing expansion and modernization projects.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: In addition, we announced plans to bring advanced HBM packaging capabilities to the United States.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: In addition to the CHIPS Act direct funding, we receive a 35% investment tax credit on qualified investments in U.S. semiconductor manufacturing under the CHIPS Act.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: We have also signed a non-binding term sheet with the State of New York that provides for up to $5.5 billion in funding for the planned four-fab facility over the next 20-plus years through a combination of tax credits for qualified capital investments and incentives for eligible new job wages.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: Outside the United States, we are investing in manufacturing technologies, facilities and equipment, and R&D, and advancing our global back-end assembly and test network.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: These investments support our product portfolio and extend our ability to meet global market demand in the future.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: Planned investments and those underway include the following:

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: India: Our assembly and test facility in Gujarat commenced commercial shipments and will start ramping production in 2026;

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: Japan: We are modernizing our Hiroshima manufacturing facility to support future DRAM nodes and AI memory production;

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: Singapore: We broke ground in January 2025 on an HBM advanced packaging facility to meaningfully expand our total advanced packaging capacity beginning in the first half of calendar 2027.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: In January 2026, we broke ground on an additional advanced wafer fab facility located within our existing NAND manufacturing complex.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: This facility will provide additional cleanroom space when it becomes operational in the second half of calendar 2028, helping address growing market demand for NAND technology driven by the rapid expansion of AI and data-centric applications; and

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: Taiwan: We are modernizing and expanding our production capacity for DRAM and HBM products to meet rising market demand.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: In March 2026, we completed the acquisition of a wafer fabrication facility in Tongluo, Miaoli County, Taiwan, from Powerchip Semiconductor Manufacturing Corporation for cash consideration of $1.8 billion.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: We expect this site to support meaningful product shipments from the existing fab beginning in mid-calendar 2027.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: Adding to the existing fab, we have begun construction of a similar-sized second cleanroom at this site.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: In certain countries outside of the U.S, we receive or expect to receive, government incentives related to our investments.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: The amounts of these government incentives generally offset a portion of our planned investments and require us to meet certain conditions in order to receive such incentives.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: Our Board of Directors has authorized the discretionary repurchase of up to $10 billion of our outstanding common stock through open-market purchases, block trades, privately-negotiated transactions, derivative transactions, and/or pursuant to Rule 10b5-1 trading plans.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: Through May 28, 2026, we had repurchased an aggregate of $7.84 billion under the authorization.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: The repurchase authorization has no expiration date, does not obligate us to acquire any common stock, and is subject to market conditions, restrictions applicable under our CHIPS Act direct funding agreements, and our ongoing determination of the best use of available cash.

text: On June 24, 2026, our Board of Directors declared a quarterly dividend of $0.15 per share, payable in cash on July 21, 2026, to shareholders of record as of the close of business on July 6, 2026.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: The declaration and payment of any future cash dividends are at the discretion and subject to the approval of our Board of Directors.

section_path: Part I Item 2 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: Our Board of Directors’ decisions regarding the amount and payment of dividends will depend on many factors, including, but not limited to, our financial condition, results of operations, capital requirements, business conditions, debt service obligations, contractual restrictions, industry practice, legal requirements, regulatory constraints, and other factors that our Board of Directors may deem relevant.

section_path: Part I Item 1
text: ITEM 1. BUSINESS

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Overview
text: Overview

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Overview
text: We are a global leader in semiconductor memory and storage, powering AI and compute-intensive applications from cloud to edge.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Overview
text: With a relentless focus on our customers, technology and product leadership, and manufacturing and operational excellence, our comprehensive portfolio of high-performance DRAM, NAND, and NOR solutions deliver the speed, efficiency, and scale today’s workloads demand, accelerating intelligence to enrich life for all.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Overview
text: We manufacture our products at wholly-owned facilities and also utilize subcontractors for certain manufacturing processes.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Overview
text: Our global network of manufacturing centers of excellence not only allows us to benefit from scale while streamlining processes and operations, but it also brings together some of the world’s brightest talent to work on the most advanced memory technology.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Overview
text: Centers of excellence bring expertise together in one location, providing an efficient support structure for end-to-end manufacturing, with quicker cycle times, in partnership with teams, such as R&D, product development, human resources, procurement, and supply chain.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Overview
text: For our locations in Singapore and Taiwan, this is also a combination of bringing fabrication and back-end manufacturing together.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Overview
text: We continue to make significant investments to develop proprietary product and process technology, which generally increases bit density per wafer and reduces per-bit manufacturing costs of each generation of product.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Overview
text: We continue to introduce new generations of products that offer improved performance characteristics, including higher data transfer rates, higher bandwidth, advanced packaging solutions, lower power consumption, improved read/write reliability, and increased memory density.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Overview
text: We face intense competition in the semiconductor memory and storage markets.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Overview
text: To remain competitive, we must continuously develop and implement new products and technologies and decrease manufacturing costs in spite of inflationary pressures, changing technologies, rapid market changes, and regulatory uncertainty.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Overview
text: Our success is largely dependent on obtaining returns on our R&D investments, efficient utilization of our manufacturing infrastructure, development and integration of advanced product and process technologies, market acceptance of our diversified portfolio of semiconductor-based memory and storage solutions, and efficient capital spending.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Products, Market, and Sales
text: Products, Market, and Sales

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Product Technologies
text: Product Technologies

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Product Technologies
text: Our product portfolio of memory and storage solutions, advanced solutions, and storage platforms is based on our high-performance semiconductor memory and storage technologies, including DRAM, NAND, and NOR.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Product Technologies
text: We sell our products through our business units into various markets in numerous forms, including components, modules, SSDs, managed NAND, multi-chip packages, and wafers.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Product Technologies
text: Many of our system-level solutions combine NAND, a controller, firmware, and in some cases DRAM.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Product Technologies
text: DRAM: DRAM products are dynamic random access memory semiconductor devices with low latency that provide high-speed data retrieval with a variety of performance characteristics.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Product Technologies
text: DRAM products lose content when power is turned off (“volatile”) and are most commonly used in the data center, client PC, graphics, industrial, mobile, and automotive markets.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Product Technologies
text: In 2025, we began shipping the industry’s first 1γ (1-gamma) production node, which is our first DRAM node incorporating EUV lithography and offers further improvements in power efficiency, performance, and bit density compared to our prior DRAM node products.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Product Technologies
text: Our 1γ DRAM node is ramping well and on track to become the highest-volume node in our history.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Product Technologies
text: The majority of our DRAM bit production in the fourth quarter of 2026 was on our leading-edge 1γ node.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Product Technologies
text: High-Bandwidth Memory (“HBM”): A 3D stacked DRAM architecture that utilizes through-silicon via connections for more efficient communication, giving it the ability to achieve a higher bandwidth while consuming less power compared to other memory types.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Product Technologies
text: This makes it ideal for applications that require high data throughput and energy efficiency, such as AI applications and high-performance computing.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Product Technologies
text: Double Data Rate (“DDR”): DDR memory transfers data twice per clock cycle, resulting in improved speeds, power efficiency, and storage density.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Product Technologies
text: DDR5 is the fifth generation of this technology and offers the critical improvements in bandwidth and power efficiency necessary to meet the growing needs of high-performance computing, AI, and data-intensive applications.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Product Technologies
text: Low-Power DRAM (“LPDDR”): Engineered for mobile devices and applications requiring low power consumption.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Product Technologies
text: LPDDR products generally operate at a lower voltage than standard DRAM products and are beneficial to any power-conscious application.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Product Technologies
text: The benefits of LPDDR memory are being realized by many market segments, including mobile, PC, automotive, and data center.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Product Technologies
text: Graphics DRAM (“GDDR”): High-performance memory solution designed for graphics cards, gaming consoles, and high-performance computing applications.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Product Technologies
text: GDDR memory is optimized for high-bandwidth workloads encountered by graphics processing units, offering faster data rates and efficient data processing capabilities.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Product Technologies
text: Total reported DRAM revenue was $100.68 billion in 2026, $28.58 billion in 2025, and $17.60 billion in 2024.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Product Technologies
text: NAND: NAND products are non-volatile, re-writable semiconductor storage devices that provide high-capacity, low-cost storage with a variety of performance characteristics.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Product Technologies
text: NAND is used in SSDs for the data center, client PC, consumer, and automotive markets, and in removable storage markets.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Product Technologies
text: Managed NAND is used in smartphones and other mobile devices, and in the consumer, automotive, and embedded markets.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Product Technologies
text: Low-density NAND is ideal for applications like automotive, surveillance, machine-to-machine, automation, printer, and home networking.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Product Technologies
text: In 2024, we began volume production of Micron G9 NAND, representative of the industry's ninth-generation 3D NAND node.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Product Technologies
text: The majority of our NAND bit production in 2026 was on leading-edge Micron G8 and G9 NAND nodes.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Product Technologies
text: Our NAND flash includes triple-level cell (“TLC”) and quad-level cell (“QLC”), each with varying levels of storage density, performance, and endurance.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Product Technologies
text: Solid State Drives (“SSDs”): SSD storage products incorporate NAND, a controller, and firmware to offer significant performance and features over hard disk drives, including smaller form factors, faster read and write speeds, higher reliability, and lower power consumption needed to address the growing demands of data-centric workloads, ever-increasing expectations of client users, and the stringent requirements of automotive and industrial applications.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Product Technologies
text: Managed NAND: Managed NAND combines NAND flash with a sophisticated controller and firmware in a single package.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Product Technologies
text: This integration allows the memory to manage itself, handling tasks like wear leveling, bad block management, and error correction internally, freeing the host system from these tasks.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Product Technologies
text: Products such as embedded MultiMediaCards (“e.MMC”) and universal flash storage (“UFS”) offer solutions that are compact and reliable, making them widely used across the mobile, automotive, and industrial markets.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Product Technologies
text: Multi-Chip Packages (“MCPs”): Designed to provide high-performance, compact, and efficient memory solutions by integrating multiple types of memory, generally LPDDR and NAND, into a single package.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Product Technologies
text: MCPs are used in embedded internet of things (“IoT”) applications, automotive systems, mobile devices, and industrial devices where space and power efficiency are critical.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Product Technologies
text: Total reported NAND revenue was $31.79 billion in 2026, $8.50 billion in 2025, and $7.23 billion in 2024.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Product Technologies
text: NOR: NOR products are non-volatile, re-writable semiconductor memory devices that provide fast read speeds.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Product Technologies
text: NOR is most commonly used for reliable code storage (e.g., boot, application, operating system, and execute-in-place code in an embedded system) and for frequently changing small data storage and is ideal for automotive, industrial, and consumer applications.

text: Marketing and Customers

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Marketing and Customers
text: We seek to build collaborative relationships with our customers to understand their unique opportunities and challenges.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Marketing and Customers
text: By engaging with our customers early in the product life cycle to identify and design features and performance characteristics into our products, we are able to manufacture products that anticipate and address our customers’ changing needs.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Marketing and Customers
text: Collaborating with our customers on their design needs in changing end markets and meeting their timelines for qualifying new products allows us to differentiate our memory and storage solutions, which provides greater value to our customers.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Marketing and Customers
text: Our semiconductor memory and storage products are offered under our Micron brand name and through private labels.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Marketing and Customers
text: We market our semiconductor memory and storage products primarily through our own direct sales force and maintain sales or representative offices to support our worldwide customer base.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Marketing and Customers
text: Our products are also offered through distributors, retailers, and independent sales representatives.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Marketing and Customers
text: Our distributors carry our products in inventory and typically sell a variety of other semiconductor products, including our competitors’ products.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Marketing and Customers
text: Our independent sales representatives obtain orders, subject to final acceptance by us, and we then make shipments against these orders directly to customers or through our distributors.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Marketing and Customers
text: We maintain inventory at locations in close proximity to certain key customers to facilitate rapid delivery of products.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Marketing and Customers

text: We also have strategic customer agreements structured as take-or-pay agreements, with binding commitments for specific contractually enforceable volumes over the multi-year contract terms.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Competitive Conditions
text: Competitive Conditions

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Competitive Conditions
text: We face intense competition in the semiconductor memory and storage markets from a number of companies, including Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd.; SK hynix Inc.; Kioxia Holdings Corporation; Sandisk Corporation; ChangXin Memory Technologies, Inc. (“CXMT”); and Yangtze Memory Technologies Co., Ltd. (“YMTC”).

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Competitive Conditions
text: Our competitors may use aggressive pricing to obtain market share.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Competitive Conditions
text: Some of our competitors are large corporations or conglomerates that may operate in jurisdictions with lower labor and compliance costs and may have a larger market share and greater resources to invest in technology, capitalize on growth opportunities, and withstand downturns in the semiconductor markets in which we compete.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Competitive Conditions
text: Consolidation of industry competitors could put us at a competitive disadvantage as our competitors may benefit from increased manufacturing scale and a stronger product portfolio.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Competitive Conditions
text: Alternatively, new entrants into the memory and storage market could have a significant adverse impact on our competitive position.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Competitive Conditions
text: We operate in different jurisdictions than our competitors and may be impacted by unfavorable changes in currency exchange rates, import/export restrictions, and other trade regulations, including tariffs.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Competitive Conditions
text: In addition, governments have provided, and may continue to provide, significant assistance, financial or otherwise, to some of our competitors or to new entrants and may intervene in support of national industries and/or competitors.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Competitive Conditions
text: As a result, we face the threat of increasing competition and DRAM and NAND oversupply due to significant investment in the semiconductor industry, including by the Chinese government and various state-owned or affiliated entities, such as CXMT and YMTC.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Competitive Conditions
text: In addition, the May 2023 decision by China’s Cyberspace Administration (the “CAC”) that critical information infrastructure operators in China may not purchase Micron products had an adverse impact on our ability to compete effectively in China and elsewhere.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Competitive Conditions
text: We intend to advance our process technology to maintain product leadership and increase bit output per wafer.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Competitive Conditions
text: In addition, our competitors may increase capital expenditures resulting in future increases in worldwide supply.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Competitive Conditions
text: We, and some of our competitors, have plans to construct new fabrication facilities and/or ramp production at existing fabrication facilities to increase supply in response to a significant increase in demand for memory products across the industry.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Competitive Conditions
text: If worldwide demand for semiconductor memory and storage does not increase or remain stable, average selling prices for our products could decline materially and could materially adversely affect our business, results of operations, or financial condition.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Competitive Conditions
text: Additionally, rapid technological change in markets we serve could contribute to shortened product life cycles and a decline in average selling prices of our products.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Competitive Conditions
text: If competitors are more successful at developing or implementing new product or process technology, their products could have cost or performance advantages.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Manufacturing
text: Manufacturing

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Manufacturing
text: We manufacture our products within our own facilities located in Taiwan, Singapore, Japan, the United States, Malaysia, China, and India and also utilize subcontractors to perform certain manufacturing processes.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Manufacturing
text: Our products are manufactured on 300mm wafers in facilities that generally operate 24 hours per day, seven days per week.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Manufacturing
text: Semiconductor manufacturing is capital intensive, requiring large investments in sophisticated facilities and equipment.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Manufacturing
text: Our DRAM, NAND, and NOR products share a number of common manufacturing processes, enabling us to leverage our product and process technology and certain resources and manufacturing infrastructure across these product lines.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Manufacturing
text: Our process for manufacturing semiconductor products is complex and involves numerous precise steps, including wafer fabrication, post-fabrication processing, assembly, and test.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Manufacturing
text: Efficient production of semiconductor products requires utilization of advanced semiconductor manufacturing techniques and effectively deploying those techniques across multiple facilities.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Manufacturing
text: The primary determinants of manufacturing cost are process line-width, 3D non-volatile layers, NAND cell levels, process complexity (including the number of mask layers and fabrication steps), and manufacturing yield.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Manufacturing
text: Other factors include the cost and sophistication of manufacturing equipment, equipment utilization, cost of raw materials and other components, labor productivity and cost, package type, cleanliness of our manufacturing environment, and utilization of subcontractors to perform certain manufacturing processes.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Manufacturing
text: As we continue to increase our production of high-value products and solutions, manufacturing costs are increasingly affected by the costs of application-specific integrated circuit controllers and other semiconductors, advanced and complex packaging configurations, and testing at progressively higher performance speeds and quality levels.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Manufacturing
text: We continuously enhance our production processes, increase bits per wafer, transition to higher density products, and utilize advanced testing and assembly processes.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Manufacturing
text: Wafer fabrication occurs in a highly controlled clean environment to minimize yield loss from contaminants.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Manufacturing
text: Despite stringent manufacturing controls, individual circuits may be non-functional or wafers may be scrapped due to equipment errors, minute impurities in materials, defects in photomasks, circuit design marginalities or defects, or contamination from airborne particles, among other factors.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Manufacturing
text: Success of our manufacturing operations depends largely on minimizing defects and improving process margin to maximize yield of high-quality circuits.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Manufacturing
text: In this regard, we employ rigorous quality controls throughout the manufacturing, screening, and testing processes.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Manufacturing
text: We continue to heighten quality control as our product offerings expand into higher-end segments that require increasing performance targets.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Manufacturing
text: Our products are manufactured and sold in both packaged form and as unpackaged bare die.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Manufacturing
text: Our packaged products include packaged die, memory modules, and system-level solutions, such as SSDs, managed NAND, and MCPs.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Manufacturing
text: We assemble many products in-house and, in some cases, outsource assembly services for certain packaged die, memory modules, SSDs, and MCPs.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Manufacturing
text: We test our products at various stages in the manufacturing process, conduct numerous quality control inspections throughout the entire production flow, and perform high-temperature burn-in on finished products.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Manufacturing
text: In addition, we use our proprietary AMBYX™ line of intelligent test and burn-in systems to perform simultaneous circuit tests of semiconductor die, capturing quality and reliability data and reducing testing time and cost.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Manufacturing
text: In recent years, we have produced an increasingly broad portfolio of products and system solutions, which enhances our ability to allocate resources to our most profitable products but also increases the complexity of our manufacturing and supply chain operations.

text: Although our product lines generally use similar manufacturing processes, our costs can be affected by frequent conversions to new products; the allocation of manufacturing capacity to more complex, smaller-volume products; and the reallocation of manufacturing capacity across various product lines.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Manufacturing

subheading: Supply Chain, Materials, and Third-Party Service Providers
text: Our supply chain and operations are dependent on the availability of materials that meet exacting standards and the use of third parties to provide us with components and services.

text: We generally have multiple sources of supply for our materials and services.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Supply Chain, Materials, and Third-Party Service Providers
subheading: Supply Chain, Materials, and Third-Party Service Providers
text: However, only a limited number of suppliers are capable of delivering certain materials, components, and services that meet our standards and, in some cases, materials, components, or services are provided by a single or sole source, and we may be unable to qualify new suppliers on a timely basis.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Supply Chain, Materials, and Third-Party Service Providers
subheading: Supply Chain, Materials, and Third-Party Service Providers
text: The availability of materials or components, such as chemicals, silicon wafers, gases, photoresists, semiconductors, substrates, lead frames, printed circuit boards, targets, and reticle glass blanks is impacted by various factors.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Supply Chain, Materials, and Third-Party Service Providers
subheading: Supply Chain, Materials, and Third-Party Service Providers

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Supply Chain, Materials, and Third-Party Service Providers

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Research and Development
text: Research and Development

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Research and Development
text: Our R&D efforts are focused primarily on development of memory and storage solutions, including our industry-leading DRAM and NAND technology, that enable continuous improvement in performance and cost structure for our products.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Research and Development
text: In 2025, we began shipping the 1γ production node, which is our first DRAM node incorporating EUV lithography.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Research and Development
text: We plan to increase EUV adoption at the 1δ (1-delta) DRAM node utilizing the latest-generation EUV tools.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Research and Development
text: These more advanced EUV tools will help us optimize both cleanroom space efficiency and patterning when scaling to 1δ and beyond.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Research and Development
text: In 2025, we also began volume production on our Micron G9 NAND node.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Research and Development
text: Development of HBM4E, our next-generation HBM product, is well underway, and we expect to ramp volume in calendar 2027.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Research and Development
text: Our HBM4E will leverage our production-proven, industry-leading 1γ DRAM technology node and is expected to deliver another step-function improvement in performance, enabling a whole new generation of AI compute platforms across the industry.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Research and Development
text: Additionally, HBM4E customization options offer us further differentiation opportunities and even deeper R&D engagement with customers.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Research and Development
text: We are also focused on developing new and fundamentally different memory structures, materials, and packages designed to facilitate our transition to next generation products.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Research and Development
text: Additional R&D efforts are concentrated on the enablement of advanced computing, storage, and mobile memory architectures and the investigation of new opportunities that leverage our core semiconductor expertise.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Research and Development
text: Product design and development efforts include HBM, DDR, LPDDR, high-capacity DRAM modules, vertically stacked DRAM products for edge and data center applications and advanced graphics DRAM; TLC and QLC NAND technologies; and storage solutions (including firmware and controllers) in SSDs; and other memory technologies and systems enabled with advanced packaging technologies.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Research and Development
text: To compete in the semiconductor memory and storage markets, we must continue to develop technologically advanced products and processes.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Research and Development
text: The continued evolution of our semiconductor product offerings is necessary to meet expected customer requirements for memory and storage products and solutions.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Research and Development
text: Our process, design, firmware, controller, package, and system development efforts occur at multiple locations across the world.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Research and Development
text: Our R&D centers are located in Boise, Idaho; San Jose, California; India; Japan; Singapore; Taiwan; Italy; Mexico; China; Germany; Malaysia; and other sites in the United States.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Research and Development
text: In 2026, we announced the establishment of Micron Research Labs, a long-horizon research institution headquartered in Boise, Idaho, supported by a planned investment of approximately $10 billion over the next decade to advance memory, compute and semiconductor manufacturing technologies.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Research and Development
text: R&D expenses vary primarily with the number of development and pre-qualification wafers processed and end-product solutions developed, personnel costs, and the cost of advanced equipment dedicated to new product and process development, such as investments in EUV lithography equipment.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Research and Development
text: Because of the lead times necessary to manufacture our products, we typically begin to process wafers before completion of performance and reliability testing.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Research and Development
text: Development of a product is deemed complete when it is qualified through internal reviews and tests for performance, functionality, and reliability.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Research and Development

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Talent Acquisition, Development, and Engagement

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Talent Acquisition, Development, and Engagement

text: Compensation and Benefits

text: Our compensation programs are designed to support our team members’ financial and personal well-being by providing a valuable return for their contributions to the Company.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Compensation and Benefits

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Culture
text: Culture

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Culture
text: At Micron, we empower a culture that reflects our core values and enables the best talent to innovate and thrive.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Culture
text: To further this mission, we have required comprehensive training for all employees on fostering a respectful workplace, free from harassment or discrimination.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Culture
text: We also train our leaders on the principles of psychological safety, enabling higher levels of trust, collaboration, and performance.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Culture
text: Recognizing the significance of mental health and well-being, we offer a global employee assistance program accessible to all team members.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Culture

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Culture

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Culture

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Health, Safety, and Well-being
text: Health, Safety, and Well-being

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Health, Safety, and Well-being
text: Proactive efforts to prevent occupational illnesses and injuries allow us to maintain a safe, healthy, and secure workplace.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Health, Safety, and Well-being
text: All of our sites have health and safety committees, which are designed to promote overall operations and communications regarding safety and to help lead and implement secure and compliant work areas.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Health, Safety, and Well-being
text: Our safety program creates a unified corporate safety culture by establishing a formal training structure and common safety practices across our global facilities.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Health, Safety, and Well-being
text: In addition to our proactive efforts on safety, our team member well-being program offers resources across our five pillars (physical, mental, social, career, and financial).

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Health, Safety, and Well-being
text: We provide services to our team members, including free mental health and counseling support, on-site and near-site fitness centers, wellness spaces and health clinics at certain Micron sites, money management and other financial education tools, and encouraging team members to form healthy habits, reduce stress, and reinforce mindfulness solutions by participating in well-being challenges and measuring their personal progress.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Health, Safety, and Well-being
text: We also provide family support for caregiving needs through various solutions, including on-site or near-site childcare centers, backup care support, and referral resources.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Health, Safety, and Well-being
text: We are a member of the Responsible Business Alliance (“RBA”), a group of leading companies focused on promoting responsible working conditions, ethical business practices, and environmental stewardship throughout our global supply chain.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Health, Safety, and Well-being
text: We strive to adhere to both our Code of Business Conduct and Ethics (available on our website, www.micron.com) and the RBA Code of Conduct, which is a demonstration of our commitment to integrity and responsible practices.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Environmental, Health, and Safety Compliance
text: Environmental, Health, and Safety Compliance

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Environmental, Health, and Safety Compliance
text: Manufacturing and sales of our products are subject to complex and evolving federal, state, local, and foreign environmental, health, safety and product laws, regulations, and expectations.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Environmental, Health, and Safety Compliance
text: We approach compliance and environmental sustainability proactively to meet applicable government regulations regarding use of raw materials and chemicals, discharges, emissions, climate change, disclosures, energy use, waste disposal and materials management, worker health and safety, and product compliance.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Environmental, Health, and Safety Compliance
text: Our approach also considers the expectations of our investors, customers, team members, community members, and other stakeholders.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Environmental, Health, and Safety Compliance
text: Compliance with the law and other obligations is a minimum expectation at Micron.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Environmental, Health, and Safety Compliance
text: Our wafer fabrication facilities conform to the requirements of the ISO 14001:2015 environmental, ISO 45001:2018 occupational health and safety, and ISO 50001:2018 energy management systems standards, supporting continuous improvement in our performance.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Environmental, Health, and Safety Compliance
text: Within these frameworks, we maintain a global environmental, health, safety, and energy policy that addresses matters such as aspect and hazard evaluation and control, compliance obligations, training, communication, document and operational control, emergency preparedness and response, and management review.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Environmental, Health, and Safety Compliance
text: While we have not experienced any material adverse effects to our operations from these laws and regulations, changes in regulations or stakeholder expectations could necessitate additional capital expenditures, modification of our operations or chemical usage, increased compliance and reporting costs, or other compliance actions.

text: Sales of our memory and storage products, and the transfer of related technical information and know-how, including support, are subject to laws and regulations governing international trade, including, but not limited to, export control, customs, and sanctions regulations administered by U.S. government agencies, such as the Bureau of Industry and Security (“BIS”) of the U.S. Department of Commerce and the Office of Foreign Asset Control of the U.S. Department of the Treasury.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Trade Regulations
text: Other jurisdictions, such as the European Union or China, also maintain, or may implement, similar laws and regulations with which we must comply.

section_path: Part I Item 1 > Trade Regulations
text: In addition, increased tariffs imposed by the countries in which our products are sold can increase the cost of our product to our customers.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
category: Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
text: Volatility in average selling prices for our semiconductor memory and storage products may adversely affect our business.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
category: Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
text: We have experienced significant volatility in our average selling prices and may continue to experience such volatility in the future due to a variety of factors, including imbalances in the supply of and demand for our products, which may be caused by circumstances that are out of our control.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
category: Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
text: Over the past five fiscal years, annual percentage changes in DRAM and NAND average selling prices have ranged from an increase of approximately 200% to a decrease of approximately 50%.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
category: Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
text: In recent periods, industry demand has outpaced supply, driving average selling prices higher, but as we and others increase supply, average selling prices may decline, particularly if demand growth slows or declines.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
category: Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
text: Conversely, in some prior periods, average selling prices for our products have been below our manufacturing costs, and we may experience such circumstances in the future.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
category: Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
text: Significant declines in average selling prices in future periods could have a material adverse effect on our business, results of operations, or financial condition.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
category: Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
text: Our gross margins may be adversely affected by a range of factors.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
category: Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
text: Our gross margins are dependent upon our average selling prices, as well as our ability to continue decreasing per gigabit manufacturing costs, which is primarily achieved through improvements in our manufacturing processes and product designs.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
category: Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
text: Factors that may limit our ability to control our per gigabit manufacturing costs at sufficient levels to prevent deterioration of or improve gross margins include, but are not limited to:

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
category: Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
text: strategic product diversification decisions affecting product mix;

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
category: Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
text: increasing complexity of our product portfolio, which may impact operational costs;

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
category: Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
text: increasing complexity of manufacturing processes;

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
category: Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
text: difficulties in transitioning to smaller line-width process technologies or additional 3D memory layers or NAND cell levels;

text: process complexity, including number of mask layers and fabrication steps;

category: Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
text: higher costs of goods and services due to, among other things, inflationary pressures, labor disputes, regulatory actions, including tariffs or trade restrictions, increased input costs, or market conditions; and

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
category: Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
text: higher manufacturing costs per gigabit due to fabrication facility underutilization, lower wafer output, and insufficient volume to run new technology nodes to achieve cost optimization.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
category: Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
text: Many factors may result in a reduction of our output or a delay in ramping production, which have in the past and could in the future lead to underutilization of our production assets.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
category: Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
text: These factors may include, among others, a weak demand environment, industry oversupply, inventory surpluses, difficulties in ramping emerging technologies, supply chain disruptions, and delays from equipment suppliers.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
category: Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
text: A significant portion of our manufacturing costs are fixed and do not vary proportionally with changes in production output.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
category: Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
text: As a result, lower utilization, lower wafer output, and corresponding increases in our per gigabit manufacturing costs could result in higher inventory carrying costs, and have had, and may in the future have, an adverse effect on our gross margins, business, results of operations, or financial condition.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
category: Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
text: We operate in a dynamic and rapidly evolving industry where the timeframes for product transitions, facility expansions, production ramps, and supply chain shifts are increasingly compressed.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
category: Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
text: To remain competitive, we must continuously develop and implement new products and technologies and decrease manufacturing costs in spite of inflationary pressures and regulatory uncertainty.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
category: Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
text: As we streamline our production and shift capacity to leading-edge nodes and, as we endeavor to increase our capacity by expanding existing facilities and building new facilities, we face execution risks that could impact our ability to meet customer demand and maintain market coverage.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
category: Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
text: There can be no assurance we will be able to do the following:

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
category: Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
text: timely identify and address technology inflections and market changes;

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
category: Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
text: accurately forecast demand and inventory levels of our customers or distributors;

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
category: Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
text: timely complete facility expansions and transitions of products to new fabrication facilities;

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
category: Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
text: timely ramp production as we transition our operations footprint to new fabrication facilities;

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
category: Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
text: maintain operational flexibility in response to unforeseen changes in customer demand; and

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
category: Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
text: maintain supply scalability during downturns in the semiconductor markets in which we compete as we streamline our product portfolio to drive further fabrication efficiencies.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
category: Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
text: Our ability to execute on multiple transitions simultaneously, while maintaining supply continuity, quality standards, and cost competitiveness, is critical to sustaining our market position.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
category: Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
text: If we do not successfully anticipate technology inflections and respond to changes in customer requirements and market changes, our business, results of operations, or financial condition could be materially adversely affected.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
category: Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
text: Any misalignment between forecasted and actual demand, or delays in ramping new technologies, could result in elevated inventory levels, underutilized capacity, and gross margin pressure.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
category: Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
text: Additionally, our customers have from time to time overstated their expected demand requirements, possibly to procure additional supply, and may do so in the future.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
category: Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
text: This could exacerbate the foregoing issues and could negatively impact our ability to forecast and to allocate supply appropriately among our customers.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
category: Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
text: We have a broad portfolio of products to address our customers’ needs, which span multiple market segments and are subject to rapid technological changes.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
category: Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
text: Our manufacturing costs on a per gigabit basis vary across our portfolio as they are largely influenced by the technology node in which the solution was developed.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
category: Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
text: We strive to balance our demand and supply for each technology node, but the dynamics of our markets and our customers can create periods of imbalance, which can lead us to carry elevated inventory levels and underutilized capacity.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
category: Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
text: Consequently, we may incur charges in connection with obsolete or excess inventories, or we may not fully recover our costs, which would reduce our gross margins.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
category: Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
text: In addition, due to the customized nature of certain products we manufacture, we may be unable to sell certain finished goods inventories to alternative customers or manufacture in-process inventory to different specifications, which may result in excess and obsolescence charges or loss of revenue in future periods.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
category: Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry
text: In addition, if we are unable to supply products that meet customer design and performance specifications, we may be required to sell such products at lower average selling prices, which may reduce our gross margins.

section_path: Part I Item 1A > Risks Related to Our Business, Operations, and Industry

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Memory and Storage Demand
text: Memory and Storage Demand

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Memory and Storage Demand
text: AI-driven memory and storage demand growth is outpacing industry supply.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Memory and Storage Demand
text: In 2026, we continued to benefit from substantial improvements in pricing and margins, reflecting strong demand growth, driven in large part by the continued advancement of AI.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Memory and Storage Demand
text: The AI-driven growth in the data center has accelerated demand for memory and storage at a rate greater than our ability and the industry’s ability to increase supply.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Memory and Storage Demand
text: This has led to decisions on supply allocation that may impact certain customers and end markets.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Memory and Storage Demand
text: Robust overall DRAM and NAND demand and constrained supply has led to increased pricing and improved the profitability across our portfolio.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Memory and Storage Demand
text: In 2025, we benefited from substantial improvements in DRAM pricing, volumes and margins as compared to 2024, reflecting strong demand growth, driven in part by the continued advancement of AI.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Memory and Storage Demand
text: During 2025, we shifted a portion of our DRAM supply to the data center and hyperscale cloud markets to meet the strong demand fueled by AI, resulting in a revenue mix weighted more prominently toward segments experiencing higher growth.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Memory and Storage Demand
text: The pivot to higher-growth segments, together with our strong execution, robust overall industry DRAM demand, and constrained supply, led to improved profitability across our DRAM portfolio.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Memory and Storage Demand
text: In 2025, NAND revenue increased from 2024 on higher bit shipments due to demand growth.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Memory and Storage Demand
text: The 2025 NAND gross margin percentage increased from 2024 due to cost reductions.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Strategic Customer Agreements
text: Strategic Customer Agreements

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Strategic Customer Agreements
text: The evolving industry landscape, characterized by strong long-term customer demand for memory solutions and structurally constrained supply growth, has elevated the strategic importance of memory to our customers’ product roadmaps.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Strategic Customer Agreements
text: As customers increasingly seek to secure committed long-term access to advanced memory technology and committed long-term memory supply, we have experienced increased customer engagement in strategic commitments.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Strategic Customer Agreements
text: In the third and fourth quarters of 2026, we entered into, and expect to continue to enter into, strategic customer agreements.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Strategic Customer Agreements
text: These agreements provide customers with contracted supply assurance and greater pricing visibility, and provide us with greater visibility and improved stability in our business performance.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Strategic Customer Agreements
text: Strategic customer agreements are structured as take-or-pay agreements, with binding commitments for specific volumes over the multi-year contract terms.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Strategic Customer Agreements
text: Pricing for our contracts is either fixed or periodically negotiated, with the majority of the strategic customer agreements having pricing that is subject to minimum and maximum bands.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Strategic Customer Agreements
text: We expect gross margins from our strategic customer agreements with price bands, even at floor pricing levels, to yield gross margins meaningfully above our peak quarterly margins in any past cycle.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Strategic Customer Agreements
text: Accordingly, we believe these agreements accelerate the transformation of our business model and will significantly enhance the durability and predictability of our financial performance.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: Liquidity and Capital Resources

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: Our primary source of liquidity is cash generated from operations.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: We also receive significant funding from government assistance and customer deposits associated with strategic customer agreements.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: In prior years, we have obtained significant financing from capital markets and financial institutions.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: Cash generated from operations is highly dependent on selling prices for our products, which can vary significantly from period to period.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: Cash and marketable investments totaled $73.45 billion as of September 3, 2026, and $11.94 billion as of August 28, 2025.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: Our cash and investments consist primarily of bank deposits, money market funds, and liquid investment-grade, fixed-income securities, which are diversified among industries and individual issuers.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: To mitigate credit risk, we invest in high-credit-quality issuers and, by policy, generally limit the concentration of credit exposure by restricting the amount of investments with any single obligor.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: To mitigate interest rate risk, we primarily invest in shorter term securities.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: As of September 3, 2026, $5.12 billion of our cash and marketable investments was held by our foreign subsidiaries.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: In 2026, we executed strategic customer agreements with a number of customers.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: These agreements included binding commitments for specific contractually enforceable volumes over the multi-year contract terms.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: Strategic customer agreements often include substantial customer deposits that are returned to the customer if the customer meets the minimum purchase commitments.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: If the customer does not meet the minimum purchase commitments, we may retain all or a portion of the deposit.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: In connection with these strategic customer agreements, we received cash deposits of $12.75 billion in 2026.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: Nearly all of the deposits are scheduled to be repaid between 2029 and 2031.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: Certain strategic customer agreements also include terms requiring our customers to maintain letters of credit with third-party financial institutions.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: Our right to access such letters of credit is contingent upon the occurrence of specified events of default or breach by our customers.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: Letters of credit are not recognized as revenue unless an event of default or breach has occurred.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: The aggregate amount of letters of credit issued, or contractually committed to be issued, by third-party financial institutions was $7 billion as of September 3, 2026.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: In the event of customer default or breach, our contractual recovery rights may include proceeds from letters of credit, rights to decrement customer deposits and other contractual remedies.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: We continuously evaluate alternatives for efficiently funding our capital expenditures and ongoing operations.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: As of September 3, 2026, $2.00 billion was available to draw under our Revolving Credit Facility.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: Funding of certain significant capital projects is also supported by the receipt of government incentives.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: Our incentives are conditioned upon achieving or maintaining certain outcomes and satisfying compliance requirements and are subject to reduction, termination, or clawback.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: To develop new product and process technology, support future growth, achieve operating efficiencies, and maintain product quality, we must continue to invest in manufacturing technologies, facilities and equipment, and R&D.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: In addition to the supply capacity we generate through our proprietary product and process technology that increases bit density per wafer, we will need to add new DRAM wafer capacity to support projected memory demand in the second half of the decade and beyond.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: Following the enactment of the CHIPS Act, we announced plans to invest in leading-edge memory manufacturing sites in Idaho and New York, based on CHIPS Act support through grants and investment tax credits.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: As part of this plan, in September 2022, we broke ground on a leading-edge memory manufacturing fab in Boise, Idaho.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: Construction of the fab began in October 2023, with first DRAM wafer output projected in mid-calendar 2027.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: In June 2025, in connection with certain amendments to our CHIPS Act agreements, we announced plans for a second leading-edge memory manufacturing fab in Idaho to serve growing market demand fueled by AI.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: Construction activities for the second Idaho fab began in 2026, and we expect initial wafer output by late calendar 2028.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: Our investment plan for New York includes construction of a leading-edge DRAM memory manufacturing site, consisting of up to four fabs to be built over the next 20-plus years, in Clay, New York.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: In January 2026, we broke ground on our first New York fab.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: In July 2026, we achieved the first concrete pour for the foundation of that fab, marking the transition from site preparation into vertical construction.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: We expect initial wafer output in calendar 2030.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: We expect these new fabs to be key to meeting our requirements for additional wafer capacity, in line with industry demand trends and our objective of maintaining stable bit share.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
text: In 2026, we launched first production starts of our 1α (1-alpha) DDR4 technology in our Manassas, Virginia, fab, which will add to our capability to support the legacy product needs of our customers in auto, industrial, medical, aerospace and defense markets.

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Liquidity and Capital Resources

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Liquidity and Capital Resources

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Liquidity and Capital Resources

section_path: Part II Item 7 > Liquidity and Capital Resources
